sentences.text: Further study revealed that the initially identified frill spikes were actually the second through fourth pairs, with the first pair being small and previously misinterpreted. Re-examination showed at least five pairs of frill spikes, a trait consistent with centrosaurines but not chasmosaurines.
Medusaceratops is distinguished from other contemporaneous ceratopsids by its unique frill ornamentation.
The genus name refers to the Greek monster Medusa, alluding to the large, thick, snake-like spikes extending from the sides of its frill.
The species name lokii honors the Norse god Loki, referencing the years of taxonomic confusion surrounding the fossils before they were named.
Canadian paleontologist Michael J. Ryan first coined the name Medusaceratops in a dissertation in 2003.
The genus was formally described by Ryan, Russell, and Hartman in 2010, with the type species Medusaceratops lokii.
New material found in 2011 and 2012 revealed skeletal traits characteristic of Centrosaurinae, confirming the dinosaur's classification.
Medusaceratops is classified within the subfamily Centrosaurinae, where it is most similar to Albertaceratops and Wendiceratops. Medusaceratops belongs to the subfamily Centrosaurinae.
Medusaceratops belongs to the tribe Albertaceratopsini.
Medusaceratops can be distinguished from other valid Judith River ceratopsids like Avaceratops, Judiceratops, and Spiclypeus by its unique frill ornamentation.
Medusaceratops lived during the Late Cretaceous (middle Campanian stage) in the Judith River Formation of Montana, USA.
The dinosaur lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, approximately between 84 and 71 million years ago.
The fossil record for Medusaceratops spans from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
It was once considered the oldest known chasmosaurine until the description of Judiceratops from a slightly older geological formation.
The initial interpretation of the frill spikes was challenged in 2018 after additional material was described.
